After another low turnout LA area election, what does it take to get people to vote?

Mary Plummer

After another low turnout LA area election, what does it take to get people to vote?

UPDATE: April 12 - The Los Angeles County Registrar's office has released certified special election results. Officials counted a total of 85,083 ballots in Assembly Districts 39, 45 and 54, with a turnout among L.A. County eligible voters of 10.8 percent. The lineup going into the general election did not change. Full L.A. County results are available at lavote.net.

The headline in Tuesday's special elections isn't the outright win captured by one state Assembly candidate or the runoffs that the top finishers in two other districts now face. 

Instead it's the low turnout in yet another Los Angeles area election. Despite accusations of sexual misconduct against the sitting lawmakers that forced their resignations in two of three districts where voters are selecting interim replacements, Los Angeles County voter participation came in at 8.23 percent based on semi-official results. 

That number may improve somewhat as remaining ballots are counted — ballots, for example, are still arriving by mail. But the turnout won't increase significantly. Election officials are expected to complete the next vote count update Friday. 

The special elections took place primarily in L.A. County where about 790,000 eligible voters reside. About 1,300 additional eligible voters live in Ventura County.

One candidate in former state Assemblyman Sebastian Ridley-Thomas' district secured more than enough votes Tuesday to win the special election for the ex-legislator's west Los Angeles seat.

Sydney K. Kamlager, district director for Democrat state Sen. Holly Mitchell, captured nearly 69 percent of the votes cast in District 54 to serve out Ridley-Thomas' remaining term that runs to December. Ridley-Thomas stepped down late last year because of health problems.

The top finishers in two other state Assembly special elections are poised to move on to runoffs in June after they failed to draw more than 50 percent of the votes needed to win outright.

Winners of the runoff elections serve until Dec. 3. A separate primary election for the next full state Assembly term, which lasts two years, also takes place on June 5. If needed, runoffs will be held in November.   

Although all three districts are solidly Democratic, Republicans did well overall and low turnout may have played a part. GOP candidates are currently second in the vote counts for Districts 39, formerly represented by Democrat Raul Bocanegra, and District 45, once represented by Democrat Matt Dababneh.

Both Bocanegra and Dababneh resigned after becoming ensnared in sexual harassment allegations.

The Republicans' showing means they are on track to make the runoff in June, where they will go head-to-head against the Democratic frontrunners. The results may reflect the strength of Republican voters: even though their numbers are declining, they more consistently show up to vote — an advantage in low-turnout elections.

Special elections have a very different dynamic than midterm elections. For example, media coverage is typically a lot less for local special elections. So yesterday's results don't portend much for this year's congressional elections, for example. 

High voter interest in the midterms is expected because major races in Southern California could help decide if Democrats can retake control of the U.S. House of Representatives. Several Republican congressional members representing districts turning more diverse are being targeted by Democrats for turnovers.

But it's difficult to predict what will get voters out to the polls short of a controversial presidential election.

Several Southern California lawmakers have been involved in sexual harassment scandals but the controversy failed to bring out more voters in the special elections.

"It doesn’t seem as though voters are making that connection between, you know, the Me Too movement and their intensity in turning out into voting and how they’re voting," said Paul Mitchell, vice president of Political Data Inc., an elections research firm.  

Mitchell said while voters seem to care a lot about the sexual harassment issue, polls show they aren’t necessarily rating female candidates higher than their male peers.

Here are the leading candidates in each district and their share of the votes cast as of the latest tally:

State Assembly District 39 

This San Fernando Valley district includes Sylmar, San Fernando, Pacoima and parts of North Hollywood. Residents lost the district's representative after Democrat Raul Bocanegra resigned late last year following sexual misconduct allegations. "While I am not guilty of any such crimes," he said at the time, "I am admittedly not perfect."

State Assembly District 45

The district stretches from Chatsworth to Calabasas, and takes in Northridge, Reseda, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills and Encino. Democrat Matt Dababneh resigned in December after a lobbyist alleged he had sexually assaulted her in a bathroom, allegations that the legislator denied. 

State Assembly District 54

On resigning in late December, Ridley-Thomas said he had undergone five surgeries and needed time to recover. Ridley-Thomas is the son of L.A. County Supervisor Mark Ridley-Thomas. 

The district runs from Westwood to south of Leimert Park, taking in Palms, Culver City and Baldwin Hills. 

This story has been updated.

Assembly candidates face the voters in special elections forced by #MeToo scandals

By Kevin Modesti

In California’s first elections of the #MeToo era, voters in parts of Los Angeles will go to the polls Tuesday to choose three new members of the state Assembly.

The two most closely watched special elections will be held in the San Fernando Valley to fill the remaining months of the terms of Democrats Raul Bocanegra and Matt Dababneh, who resigned from their Assembly seats late last year after multiple women accused them of sexual misconduct.

The third will be held in Los Angeles, Culver City and Inglewood to fill out the term of Democrat Sebastian Ridley-Thomas, who cited health problems in resigning from the Assembly at the end of last year.

Female candidates loom prominently in all three races at a time when more women than usual are running for offices of all kinds, a trend that’s seen as a reaction to sexual-harassment scandals in government, women’s anger at Trump administration policies, and backlash from Hillary Clinton’s presidential election loss.

Whether voters will lean toward women in Tuesday’s elections isn’t clear.

“The subset of voters who are likely to vote in a special election tend to be focused on other issues,” said Tom Hogen-Esch, a political science professor at Cal State Northridge. “They’re older, they’re whiter, they’re going to be more conservative than the area as a whole, and they’re going be people who are directly impacted by the election, whether they’re public employees or people with stakes in issues in the Legislature.”

Special-election results can be unpredictable, Hogen-Esch said, because relatively few voters participate. In recent years, stand-alone special elections in L.A. County have typically drawn less than 10 percent of registered voters. Adding to the unpredictability is the brevity of the campaigns, only seven weeks from the release of the certified candidates list to election day.

Polls will be open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. Mail-in voting began March 6. L.A. County election information is available at lavote.net.

In each election, if any candidate receives more than 50 percent of the votes, he or she will be sworn in to serve until Dec. 3. If not, the top two in Tuesday’s returns will advance to a runoff on June 5. The primary for the next full two-year term in each Assembly office will also be held June 5 as part of a full ballot of statewide, state legislative and congressional contests.

In one of the three Assembly districts holding special elections, the potential for surprise is heightened by the presence of two unorthodox candidates.

That’s District 45, covering the west San Fernando Valley communities of Calabasas, Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills, West Hills, Winnetka, Northridge, Reseda, Tarzana and Encino and the Ventura County community of Bell Canyon. Eight candidates are seeking Dababneh’s seat.

It’s a heavily Democratic district — as are the other two — and six candidates are Democrats: attorney and leaving campaign fundraiser Jesse Gabriel, L.A. City Council aide Tricia Robbins Kasson, L.A. School Board aide Ankur Patel, Ray Bishop, Jeff Bornstein and Daniel Brin. But the ballot also includes Republican Justin Clark, a 19-year-old CSUN student, and independent Dennis Zine, a conservative former L.A. city councilman who announced his withdrawal from the race in February but says he would serve if elected.

Despite his youth, Clark said he’s “very confident” of finishing in the top two and making a runoff, in part because he believes he’ll get most Republicans’ votes while the Democratic candidates are splitting liberal votes. Similar math could help Robbins Kasson, the only woman in the race.

In District 39, including the northeast San Fernando Valley communities of Arleta, Lake View Terrace, Mission Hills, North Hollywood, Pacoima, Sun Valley, Sunland-Tujunga, Sylmar and San Fernando, six candidates hope to replace Bocanegra. Five of them are Democrats: former Assemblywoman Patty Lopez, engineer and educator Luz Rivas, union workforce development director Antonio Sanchez, former Assembly staffer and community volunteer Yolie Anguiano and documentary filmmaker Patrea Patrick. The lone Republican is Ricardo Benitez.

Lopez’s presence is a reminder of the political surprises and turmoil that have become commonplace in the northeast Valley. A school and church volunteer and political novice, Lopez upset Bocanegra in the 2014 election and served two years in the Assembly before Bocanegra avenged the defeat in 2016.

In District 54, covering parts of L.A. and the Westside, four candidates vie to replace Ridley-Thomas. Three are Democrats: Sydney Kamlager, president of the L.A. Community College District Board of Trustees and the race’s top fundraiser; Tepring Piquado, a neuroscientist and Rand Corporation policy analyst, and Grayson Pangilinan, a 23-year-old green energy entrepreneur. One is Republican: small business owner Glen Ratcliff.

It’s expected that one of the women will emerge as the winner.

Bocanegra and Dababneh are two of several California legislators — all L.A. County Democrats — accused of sexual harassment since allegations against Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein touched off the #MeToo movement of women speaking out about mistreatment by powerful men.

State Sen. Tony Mendoza of Arleta resigned in February amid harassment allegations but plans to run in a special election scheduled for June 5 in District 32. Sen. Bob Hertzberg of Van Nuys was reprimanded. Assemblywoman Cristina Garcia of Bell Gardens is under investigation.

Credit: By Kevin Modesti | kmodesti@scng.com | Daily News

Comparing the candidates in Tuesday’s Assembly District 45 special election

By Kevin Modesti

//s3.amazonaws.com/js-cache/16dbc8c14acdb8703b.js Here’s a voters’ guide to the eight candidates in the special election Tuesday, April 3, to fill the remaining months of Matt Dababneh’s term representing Assembly District 45, covering the west San Fernando Valley communities of Calabasas, Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills, West Hills, Winnetka, Northridge, Reseda, Tarzana and Encino and the Ventura County community of Bell Canyon. Dababneh resigned because of sexual-misconduct allegations. Candidates are listed in randomly selected ballot order. (A voters’ guide for the special election in Assembly District 39, in the northeast San Fernando Valley, appeared in Sunday’s Daily News.)

ASSEMBLY DISTRICT 45 JUSTIN CLARK Party: Republican Background: The lone Republican in the race, running “to restore common sense to Sacramento,” is an 18-year-old Cal State Northridge student who works in an ice cream shop. “I do not have some long history in public service,” his website says.

Backers: Clark does not list endorsements, and staff officials list no fundraising reports for his campaign. Big idea: Clark says he will put constituents’ interests first, and complains that “Sacramento is plagued by corruption and those whose first duty is to special interest groups or their party.”

Website: www.votejustinclark.com TRICIA ROBBINS KASSON Party: Democratic Background: An aide to Los Angeles City Councilman Bob Blumenfield, Robbins Kasson has played a role in revitalization of commercial corridors in Canoga Park and Reseda, and touts her experience on issues of community planning, transportation and housing.

Backers: Robbins Kasson has a long list of endorsements from state lawmakers and L.A. City Council members, and women’s political groups.

Big idea: The only woman in this race, Robbins Kasson says electing more women to positions of power is needed to change a culture of sexual harassment in California government. “I believe when you have more women who are part of the conversations, it shifts the conversations,” she said.

Website: www.tricia4assembly.com JESSE GABRIEL Party: Democratic Background: Gabriel, a constitutional-rights and general-litigation attorney with Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, has worked on lawsuits to protect undocumented young people known as Dreamers from Trump administration efforts to roll back DACA protections.

Backers: Gabriel’s big endorsements come from the Democratic Party of the San Fernando Valley and an array of L.A.-area Democratic members of Congress.

Big idea: Gabriel’s calling card is his work on lawsuits against the Trump administration, more than promises about specifically local issues. “We must stand up to the Trump administration to protect our people and our planet,” he says in a campaign mailer.

Website: https://jesseforassembly.com ANKUR PATEL Party: Democratic Background: An aide to an L.A. Unified School Board member, Patel calls himself “the education candidate.” He also has worked with health-care workers and tenants unions and environmental groups. He ran for the school board in 2015. Backers: Patel’s big endorsements come from progressive Democratic groups and teachers unions. Website: https://ankurforassembly.com DANIEL BRIN Party: Democratic Background: President of the West Hills Neighborhood Council, Brin is a journalist who produces publications for labor unions and health-plan trust funds, and earlier ran Jewish community newspapers.

Website: http://danielbrin.com JEFF BORNSTEIN Party: Democratic Background: Bornstein owns an electronics company. He ran previously for the L.A. City Council and for city controller. Backers: Bornstein does not claim endorsements and has not reported campaign donations.

RAY BISHOP Party: Democratic Background: Bishop has owned a variety of small businesses over the years, including a comedy club in Encino, and has been a film producer.

Backers: Bishop does not claim endorsements. His campaign donations come from individuals.

SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Los Angeles-area voters go to the polls Tuesday in special elections to fill three open Assembly seats. Two spots are vacant because lawmakers resigned amid harassment claims, potentially making room for more female lawmakers, but candidates say issues related to sexual misconduct at the Capitol aren't topof-mind for many voters.

Assemblymen Raul Bocanegra and Matt Dababneh resigned amid sexual misconduct accusations, while Sebastian Ridley-Thomas quit citing health issues.

Women could replace all three. At least one female contender in each race has a well-funded campaign.

In interviews, female candidates said it's important to have women in the Legislature but pointed to their leadership credentials as their main qualifications.

If any candidate wins more than 50 percent of the vote Tuesday — an unlikely scenario with crowded fields in all three districts — they win outright. Otherwise the top-two finishers, regardless of party, will advance to a June runoff.

The runoff contests would coincide with the statewide primary June 5.

Seven candidates are vying to replace Bocanegra, who resigned after multiple women said he kissed or groped them without consent. He said he was not guilty of any crimes against the women.

Luz Rivas, a nonprofit founder and engineer, and Antonio Sanchez, a workforce development director, are the race's leading fundraisers.

Former Assemblywoman Patty Lopez, who won the seat from Bocanegra in 2014 before he defeated her and secured the spot again in 2016, also is running.

"Some of them don't know the reason he resigned," she said. "I think people want their state legislator to focus on the issues that affect their day-to-day lives."

Sanchez said the allegations against Bocanegra rarely come up in his conversations with voters, who seem primarily concerned with high housing costs.

time.

Democrats Ankur Patel, Daniel Brin, Jeff Bornstein and Ray Bishop are also in the race. Dennis Zine, a no-partypreference candidate, will appear on the ballot but has announced he isn't campaigning. The Florida school shooting shifted many voters' attention to gun safety, said Larry Levine, who works on Robbins Kasson's campaign. But he said many are still concerned about the Dababneh allegations.

Dennis Zine dropped out of Valley Assembly race. Or did he?

By Kevin Modesti

Calvin Coolidge said, “I do not choose to run.” Lyndon Johnson said, “I shall not seek, and I will not accept, the nomination of my party for another term as your president.”

Dennis Zine’s declaration that he is not a candidate for office is less straightforward.

This is causing confusion and no small amount of concern among contenders for the Tuesday, April 3, special election for the California Assembly in the west San Fernando Valley.

Although the former Los Angeles city councilman announced in February that he was dropping out of the 45th District Assembly race, his famous name remains on the ballot and it’s conceivable he’ll receive enough votes to qualify for a runoff or help to determine who does.

On Tuesday, Zine told a reporter he is not raising funds, not campaigning, not advertising and not participating in debates. But he said that if he were to win, he would go to Sacramento and serve the remaining months of the term of Matt Dababneh, who resigned from the Assembly in December after being accused of sexual misconduct.

“I’m not going to slap the voters in the face. If they call me to serve, I’ll serve. It’s like when I was eligible for the draft,” Zine said. “I’d be honored to serve. I look at the state and the trouble with taxation and homelessness. I’m the only candidate without a party affiliation [he’s listed on the ballot with ‘no party preference’], so I’d work with both parties.” If nobody gets an outright majority April 3 and Zine qualifies for the runoff June 5, would he campaign for that election? If he won the special election, would he file to run for the next full two-year term as a write-in candidate on Nov. 6 against the two who advance from the top-two primary, also to be held June 5?

“I will face that [decision] when I come to it,” Zine said.

So he’s not saying: Don’t vote for me. But he’s also not saying: Vote for me.

The ambiguity adds to the mystery, conjecture about Zine’s true motive, and the expectation that the man nicknamed Z Man will be the X factor in the election.

The 45th District election — one of three Assembly special elections April 3 — drew eight candidates: Democrats Jesse Gabriel, Tricia Robbins Kasson, Ankur Patel, Ray Bishop, Jeff Bornstein and Daniel Brin, Republican Justin Clark, and Zine. In a district where Democrats outnumbered Republicans 49 percent to 22 percent in January voter registration figures, Clark could benefit from being the only Republican and qualify for the runoff. This, despite the fact that Clark is, as his campaign website says, “an 18-year-old college student currently attending California State University Northridge while also working at a local ice cream shop.”

It’s also possible that conservative voters will skip over young Clark and choose old Zine, who has been a registered Republican and independent, and was the most boisterous non-liberal voice on the City Council.

“He’s a factor, for sure,” said Robbins Kasson, an aide to L.A. City Councilman Bob Blumenfield, Zine’s successor on the council.

Zine, 70, surprised many when he announced Jan. 29 that he would run for the Assembly five years after his last bid for office, a losing race for L.A. city controller following 12 years on the council. He surprised even more when he announced Feb. 12 that he had quit the race to accept what campaign consultant Rick Taylor called another “great opportunity.” Zine has yet to identify that other great opportunity. (He said Tuesday he has promised that scoop to the publisher of the Warner Center News, a community weekly for which Zine writes a column.)

When Zine announced his withdrawal, rivals speculated that he wasn’t really giving up on the race, but was hoping to coast on his name recognition while avoiding negative publicity stemming from an old sexual-harassment accusation. In 1999, when he was a director of the L.A. police union, Zine was accused by a female LAPD officer of making inappropriate advances during a business trip. An LAPD disciplinary board absolved Zine but criticized him for “unbelievably poor judgment.”

Denying that his lack of a campaign is itself a campaign tactic, Zine said: “When I withdrew, I withdrew. I thought they’d take me off the ballot. I didn’t know the rules. The secretary of state said the only way we take you off is if you die.” This was a length to which Zine was unwilling to go.

Gabriel, the race’s leading fundraiser, said he believes Zine. All the same, Gabriel’s campaign sent out a mailer reminding voters that Zine dropped out. And California Charter Schools Association Advocates, which has made independent expenditures in support of Gabriel, has spent more than $36,000 this month on advertising opposing Zine.

A recent mailer to some voters from the charter-schools group proclaimed: “Important News for Dennis Zine Supporters: Dennis Zine Has Withdrawn From the Race for Assembly.”

Zine received one of those mailers at his west Valley home, and said he thought: “Obviously there was a poll done that shows somebody’s concerned about Dennis P. Zine.”

Gabriel campaign consultant Mac Zilber said he did commission a poll, but wouldn’t say what it revealed.

Zine said he plans to return the campaign contributions he has received after paying off small expenses from the two weeks his campaign was afloat.

On April 3, while most candidates await election returns with campaign advisers and supporters, Zine said he won’t be “sitting there looking at the numbers.” As for what he will be doing, he said, “I haven’t looked at my calendar.” “It is unusual,” Zine said of the whole scene.

That, everyone could agree, is clear.

California State Assembly candidates face questions about their San Fernando Valley roots

By Kevin Modesti

California law says members of the state Legislature must live in the districts they represent. It doesn’t say how long they must have lived there.

So nothing is illegal about the fact that Democrats Luz Rivas and Antonio Sanchez, leading candidates in a special election for the state Assembly on April 3, moved into their northeast San Fernando Valley district in December, or that Democrat Jesse Gabriel, a contender in another special election for the Assembly the same day, has lived in his west Valley district only since July.

But that hasn’t stopped other candidates with deeper roots here from claiming that their prominent opponents lack the local knowledge needed to promote Valley residents’ interests in Sacramento.

“Jesse moved into the district seven months ago. He doesn’t know Valley issues,” said Democrat Tricia Robbins Kasson, a 39-year resident of the Valley and one of eight candidates on the ballot in Assembly District 45, where voters will fill the vacancy created when Matt Dababneh resigned following sexual-misconduct accusations.

A similar claim, about Sanchez and Rivas, was made by Dreatemocrat Patty Lopez, a 38-year Valley resident and one of six candidates running to fill the Assembly District 39 seat left open when Raul Bocanegra quit amid sexual-harassment allegations.

“I see this [Assembly] position being taken away by people who just moved into our district, [who] don’t know our district,” Lopez said. “They feel like, ‘Oh, I have money and power and I can take this seat.’ ”

Such rhetoric could sway some voters in the San Fernando Valley, where residents sometimes feel protective of their area, believing it receives less attention than downtown Los Angeles and West L.A. get from government leaders. Robbins Kasson, a Tarzana resident and aide to L.A. City Councilman Bob Blumenfield, said Gabriel, who lives in Encino and is a constitutional rights attorney, shows a lack of focus on west Valley issues by sending campaign mailers that highlight his role in lawsuits against the Trump administration’s plan to deport DACA recipients. Robbins Kasson political consultant Larry Levine accused Gabriel of trying to “trick” Valley voters by saying he “attended local public schools.” “He’s positioning himself as a resistance fighter against the federal government. We’re running for the state Assembly representing the southwest San Fernando Valley,” said Robbins Kasson, whose campaign emphasizes her work on the revitalization of Reseda and Canoga Park business districts.

Lopez, a San Fernando resident who served in the Assembly from 2014 to 2016 and is a long-time volunteer in area schools, churches and other organizations, says Rivas and Sanchez have done little to help the northeast Valley. “Luz has been endorsed by [L.A. Mayor Eric] Garcetti. Antonio is endorsed by the unions,” Lopez said. “Why do you have to use those big endorsements” if you’re known in the community?

But the details aren’t as clear-cut as Robbins Kasson and Lopez make it sound.

Gabriel grew up in Oak Park, in Ventura County, and attended Oak Park High School, four exits west of the 45th District line along Highway 101. Gabriel said he took courses, including a constitutional law class, at Pierce College of Woodland Hills, in the district, when he was a high school senior. He, his wife and two young children lived in Santa Monica between a stint in Washington, D.C., and their move to Encino. They’re members of Valley Beth Shalom in Encino.

“I think they’re [Robbins Kasson and Levine] trying to spin it into something,” Gabriel said. “I don’t know how you demonstrate your connection to a community more than by saying ‘We’re going to put down roots here, this is where we want to raise our kids, this is where we want to spend our life.’

“With everything going on in this country and this state, and all the issues facing the Valley, if they want to talk about the fact I went to high school five miles outside the district, that’s their choice,” said Gabriel, who has endorsements from the Democratic Party of the San Fernando Valley and the San Fernando Valley Young Democrats.

Rivas grew up in the 39th District communities of Pacoima, San Fernando and Arleta before leaving the area to earn degrees from MIT and Harvard and work in Chicago and New York. She returned to found the Pacoima-based nonprofit DIY Girls, promoting science and technology education for girls. She had a rent-control apartment in Mid-City L.A. before coming back to live in the 39th District for the first time in eight years by moving to North Hollywood in December. “We [Rivas and Lopez] represent different paths for people in our community,” Rivas said. “I wanted to explore, and I did that. I see great things about my community, and I see things I want to improve. It’s because I’ve had different experiences and perspectives. A lot of families in our community want this for their child.”

Sanchez was born in Chicago and moved to Mexico with his family before coming to the 39th District when he was 6, living in North Hollywood and then Pacoima. Recounting his boyhood, he mentions all the streets he walked to get to school. He said he and his wife moved to North Hollywood in December after three years outside the district.

“I know the district. I grew up in the district,” Sanchez said.

Other candidates in District 39 (which includes Arleta, Lake View Terrace, Mission Hills, North Hollywood, Pacoima, Sun Valley, Sunland-Tujunga, Sylmar and San Fernando) are Democrats Yolie Anguiano and Patrea Patrick, and Republican Ricardo Benitez. Also on the ballot in District 45 (Calabasas, Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills, West Hills, Winnetka, Northridge, Reseda, Tarzana, Encino and Bell Canyon) are Democrats Ankur Patel, Ray Bishop, Jeff Bornstein and Daniel Brin; Republican Justin Clark, and independent Dennis Zine (who officially dropped out of the race Feb. 12). Another special election April 3, in L.A.’s Assembly District 54, seeks a replacement for Sebastian Ridley-Thomas, who resigned citing health problems.

In each race, if nobody receives an outright majority, the top two vote-getters will advance to a June 5 runoff. The winners will serve until Dec. 3.

Politics - April 3 election poised to be big - L.A.-area turnout, backing for women could point to trends

By Kevin Modesti

Los Angeles Daily News · 2018-03-25 · Section: News · Page 1 · 1043 words

Already anticipating high-stakes state and congressional races later this year, California politics-watchers might overlook next week’s elections to fill three empty Assembly seats in the Los Angeles area.

Maybe they should pay more attention.

The April 3 special elections mark the first round of voting in 2018 in Southern California, and they might tell a lot about what to expect from future contests in a year when many of the region’s congressional races carry the po tential to reshape national politics.

Political observers say they’ll be watching the special elections for clues about several trends: • How female candidates will fare in the wake of sexual-harassment scandals, including incidents in Sacramento that created two of the Assembly openings by prompting the resignations of San Fernando Valley Democrats Raul Bocanegra and Matt Dababneh.

• Whether progressive Democrats, or moderate Democrats, run stronger in a year of party infighting following Hillary Clinton’s presidential election defeat.

• And whether liberal voters will be as enthusiastic as forecast in California’s first bunch of elections since Donald Trump’s inauguration.

“If our people are showing up for every election, that’s got to bode well for the future,” said Zack Czajkowski, who is campaign manager for Katie Hill, one of the Democrats running for Congress against Republican Rep. Steve Knight of Santa Clarita.

Czajkowski said he’s watching the April Assembly elections, which normally would attract only local interest, for clues about how women and progressive candidates — such as Hill — will do in the June 5 primary and the Nov. 6 general election.

Valerie McGinty, founder and president of Fund Her, an organization that raises money to elect progressive women to California state offices, said she has high hopes for the group’s endorsed candidates in the three Assembly special elections: Luz Rivas, Tricia Robbins Kasson and Sydney Kamlager.

“I think there’s a very good chance for all three of these candidates,” McGinty said.

She thinks they could create momentum for women to pick up as many as 10 seats that have been held by men in the Assembly and Senate, raising women’s share of the state Legislature from the present 22 percent. The prominence of women candidates is something the three April elections have in common.

• In Assembly District 39, which includes the northeast San Fernando Valley communities of Arleta, Lake View Terrace, Mission Hills, North Hollywood, Pacoima, Sun Valley, Sunland-Tujunga, Sylmar and San Fernando, the six candidates to serve the remaining months of Bocanegra’s term include four women. The winner almost certainly

will come from among five Democrats.

Union-backed Antonio Sanchez is the race’s leading fundraiser, but Rivas, the MIT- and Harvard-educated founder of a local nonprofit that supports girls’ science and technology education, has endorsements from the California Democratic Party and L.A. Mayor Eric Garcetti, and Patty Lopez can tap into the support that gave her an upset win over Bocanegra in 2014 before Bocanegra won back the Assembly seat in 2016.

• In AD 45, Robbins Kasson is the only women among eight candidates to replace Dababneh in representing the west San Fernando Valley communities of Calabasas, Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills, West Hills, Winnetka, Northridge, Reseda, Tarzana and Encino and the Ventura County community of Bell Canyon. That should give Robbins Kasson, an aide to L.A. City Councilman Bob Blumenfield, a mathematical advantage because voters who favor women in the year of #MeToo are likely to choose her. But to win, she’ll have to overcome heavy fundraising by fellow Democrat Jesse Gabriel, an attorney endorsed by the Democratic Party of the San Fernando Valley. An X factor is Dennis Zine, a well-known former L.A. city councilman who dropped out of the race but remains on the ballot, listed as an independent, one of two non-Democrats.

• In AD 54, two Democratic women lead the way in fundraising and endorsements among four candidates to replace Sebastian Ridley-Thomas, who cited health problems in his resignation, representing parts of L.A. and West L.A. as well as Culver City and Inglewood.

It seems virtually certain that Kamlager, president of the L.A. Community College District Board of Trustees, or Tepring Piquado, a neuroscientist and Rand Corp. policy analyst, will win the seat. Kamlager leads in fundraising and endorsements, with U.S. Sen. Kamala Harris her most powerful backer.

In each special election, any candidate who earns an outright majority of votes April 3 will be sworn in to serve until Dec. 3. Otherwise, the top two will advance to a runoff June 5.

Perhaps confusingly for voters, June 5 is also the day of the primary for the next full two-year term. So the same ballot booklet could include two separate races in the same district, the special-election runoff to decide who serves the remainder of the current terms and the primary to determine which two candidates advance to the Nov. 6 general election.

Some observers say it will be risky to draw conclusions from the special-election results because of the brevity of the campaigns, the Democratic leanings of the three districts, the sexual-misconduct scandals giving extra energy to women candidates, and the differences in scale between races for state Legislature and Congress. It’s also likely that voter turnout will be much lower in April than it will be in June.

“I don’t find them particularly relevant ,” said Nicole DeMont, campaign manager for Bryan Caforio, one of Katie Hill’s Democrat rivals in the congressional race against Steve Knight. The Knight-held seat is one of a half-dozen in Southern California that Democrats hope to pick up in a national effort to capture control of the House. But others say April 3 could be telling precisely because turnout is expected to be so low.

In the past five years, stand-alone special elections for state Legislature seats in L.A. County have drawn between 6.2 percent and 10.3 percent of registered voters.

If turnouts rise over 10 percent this time, it could be a sign that Democrats are unusually fired up. If that happens, campaign strategists for June and November races might change their assumptions about who is and isn’t going to vote, and broaden the targets for their messages.

For now, the easy trend to watch is how women candidates fare and whether women voters turn out more than usual. Seven women are among 18 candidates in the special elections — a higher percentage than usual. kmodesti@scng.com @KevinModesti on Twitter

Assembly race kicks off

By Ian Bradley

ISSUE-ORIENTED—Candidates meet in a debate for the 45th California Assembly District election April 3. IAN BRADLEY/Acorn Newspapers

The race is on to fill the 45th Assembly District seat vacated in January by Democrat Matt Dababneh, accused of sexual misconduct while in office.

The West Valley Chamber of Commerce hosted a forum on Feb. 21 to introduce the seven candidates who will appear on the ballot in a special election on April 3.

The two-hour event was held at the West Valley-Warner Center Chamber of Commerce in Woodland Hills. More than 100 people attended and heard the candidates answer questions about homelessness, gun violence and the future of water in the state, among other issues.

Six of the candidates are Democrats: Los Angeles City Council aide Tricia Robbins Kasson, activist Ankur Patel, attorney Jesse Gabriel, West Hills Neighborhood Council president Daniel Brin, and business owners Jeff Bornstein and Ray Bishop. The lone Republican is 18-year-old Cal State Northridge student Justin Clark.

Moderator Sean McCarthy raised the issue of campus gun violence. The candidates suggested solutions such as better background checks and measures to keep mentally ill people from obtaining firearms. Most of the candidates said they support an all-out ban on assault weapons.

Clark said many schools have programs to address potential gun violence, but need funding to use them, something he would work for. He also said gun-owning parents have a responsibility to teach their children about gun safety and to make sure they can’t cannot access weapons in the home.

Patel, who works for Los Angeles Unified School District board member Scott Schmerelson, said schools conducting random searches of students isn’t enough and that there needs to be a better framework for identifying troubled kids. Robbins Kasson said schools need staff equipped to identify and counsel students who could commit acts of violence.

Gabriel said lawmakers need to do everything they can to prevent school shootings. He said he supports an assault weapons ban and said he would address the influx of guns from states with more relaxed ownership laws, such as Arizona and Nevada.

Bornstein said the first thing he did when he arrived for the event was map out an exit strategy, which he called an unfortunate adaptation to the regularity of gun violence. He called for more gun buy-backs and better background checks.

The candidates all agreed something needed to be done to address harassment in the state government—several representatives have left office after being accused of sexual misconduct, including Dababneh, who represented the 45th district until Jan. 1, when he stepped down. In December, several women came forward to accuse him of harassment. Dababneh, a San Fernando Valley native, was elected to the seat in 2013 when he won a special election that was held after then-representative Bob Blumenfield left office to become a member of the Los Angeles City Council.

Dababneh’s term would have lasted through the end of 2018. There will be a special election on April 3 to determine who will represent the district for the rest of the year. Whoever wins the race will have to run for re-election shortly after. The seat is one of the many that will be on the ballot in the November election.

To win the special election, a candidate must receive over 50 percent of the vote. If no winner is selected, there will be another vote in June, on the same day as the primary elections. All seven of the candidates are registered for the special election and the primary.

The California Assembly’s 45th district covers an area that includes Calabasas, Bell Canyon Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills, Tarzana, West Hills, Winnetka, Encino, Northridge and Reseda.

ENCINO — With major policy differences still developing, leading candidates in a California Assembly race in the west San Fernando Valley offered a range of proposals on the timely issues of gun control and sexual harassment Tuesday in the first debate since the special-election ballot was set.

The seat represents an area that includes Calabasas, Hidden Hills, Canoga Park, Woodland Hills, West Hills, Winnetka, Northridge, Reseda, Tarzana, Encino and the Ventura County community of Bell Canyon.

Asked by moderator Jessica Levinson, a Loyola Law School professor, for proposals to reduce gun violence after the shooting deaths of 17 people at a Florida high school last week, candidates identified a variety of causes. And they suggested general solutions, including better measures to keep firearms out of the hands of mentally ill people, more safety training and safe storage of guns in households, loosing restrictions on study of gun violence by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Gabriel, the leading fundraiser in the race, said policymakers “need to do everything we can” about gun violence. “When I went to school, I worried about pop quizzes, I worried about whether my clothes fit the right way, if I was going to fit in. It’s crazy to now that I’m going to have to worry that my kids are going to go to school and I’ll have to worry about whether somebody’s going to commit a horrific act of gun violence,” Gabriel told a crowd of about 70 chambers of commerce members attending a $30-a-plate luncheon.

Robbins Kasson called for more gun buybacks, gun-purchase waiting periods and background checks, and limits on ammunition magazines.

Patel called for better steps to identify troubled youth and to keep guns from domestic violence perpetrators. Asked how well the California Legislature is responding to the Sacramento sexual-misconduct scandal that has cost two lawmakers their job and forced two others to take leaves of absence, several candidates praised the leadership of Assemblywoman Laura Friedman, D-Glendale, author of one of the bills that help harassment victims. Gabriel said changing a culture of sexual harassment in the state capitol requires electing a new generation of legislators. Brin said victims need a safe place to report harassment. Ankur Patel throws in bid for state assembly in California

By Staff Writer

News India-Times · 2018-02-16 · Section: BREAKING NEWS · 668 words

NEW YORK – Ankur Patel is running for the 45th state assembly in California, according to the California State University Northridge website.

Patel, the 32-year-old LAUSD Community Coordinator, and an Indian American, who graduated from California State University Northridge with his master's degree in 2014, has had his hands in politics for nearly a decade now as he ran for Los Angeles City Controller in 2013 and was a candidate for the LAUSD board the year after. Although he lost both races, Patel was keen to run for the 45th state assembly.

"When I was eleven years old my father ran for Congress. While he cherished the opportunities America provided our family, he knew there was a clear imbalance between the people with power and those of us without," Patel states on his website.

"My father didn't win when he ran for Congress, but the experience taught me a lot. A candidate shouldn't run for office because they believe they have a few good ideas, the backing of big dollars, or they see a political opportunity. A candidate should run for office when they believe they can represent the vision of their community," he adds.

According to Balletopedia, Patel received his bachelor's degree in ecology behavior and evolution from the University of California at Los Angeles and as well as his master's degree from California State University at Northridge.

After earning his bachelor's, Patel spent a year teaching English to young children in South Korea and then spent another six months teaching English to professionals and university students in China, according to Balletopedia. When he studied at UCLA, Patel learned about the impact that human activities had on the local and global environment and began getting involved in environmental and political campaigns, according to his website. "I remember being out on campus or on the street, clipboard in hand, asking people, 'Do you have a minute for the environment?' It was an innocent start, much like my father's, but where beliefs turned to action was during the Aliso Canyon Gas blowout in 2015," he states on his website.

"As the School and Community Coordinator for LAUSD Board Member Scott Schmerelson, I spent day after night listening to parents, teachers, and community members about the ongoing blowout, and the health symptoms experienced by people across the area. Students and teachers were getting sick, and for the first month not many government agencies were responding to the scale of the crisis. It was not a quick or easy task, but we relocated two schools over the winter break to ensure the safety of the faculty and students. I'm proud of the work we did to protect people and the integrity of our public schools, and I will bring that same ethic of listening and acting to the Assembly," he adds.

If elected, along with focusing on healthcare and the environment, Patel wants to do something about education. "One of the things that my father and my family have always emphasized is the importance of education. We need people who are going to prioritize education at the state level. CSU's are the engine for the growth and the capacity and the building of the state of California," Patel told California State University Northridge.

On his website Patel talks about his experience in China stating how "this experience was transformative, and gave me a direct perspective on the important work teachers do, and the requirements for student success in the classroom," and also served as treasurer of the Northridge East Neighborhood Council, representing his community to the City of Los Angeles, while he was working on his master's degree.

According to the Los Angeles Daily News, Patel will be running along with Justin Clark (R), Tricia Robbins Kasson (D), Jesse Gabriel (D), Daniel Brin (D), Jeff Bornstein (D), Ray Bishop (D) and former City Council member and officer Dennis Zine.

The April 3 election will determine who will replace Matt Dababneh, who resigned in December after being accused of sexual misconduct, according to the Los Angeles Daily News.

By Kevin Modesti

Only two weeks after he sprang a surprise by declaring his candidacy for the California Legislature, Dennis Zine produced a shocker by announcing it’s over.

The former Los Angeles city councilman said Monday afternoon that he’s quitting the race for an April 3 special election in the west San Fernando Valley Assembly seat left vacant when Matt Dababneh resigned in December amid sexualmisconduct allegations. “I will be announcing shortly a great opportunity that has come my way at the professional level, and I would like to thank my supporters, especially those from the 3rd Los Angeles Council District,” Zine said in a two-paragraph statement. Rival candidate Tricia Robbins Kasson complained about that proposed description, and state election officials said that designation violated ballot rules. Zine’s campaign said about noon Monday that he would instead run without a description.

Three hours later, Zine wasn’t running at all.

Taylor said Zine’s withdrawal had nothing to do with how his campaign was going in the two weeks since the 70-year-old entered the race.

Zine, a City Council member from 2001 to 2013, when he lost a bid for L.A. city controller, faced questions about sexual harassment allegations lodged against him by a female LAPD officer in 1999, when he was a police union director. Zine’s name will remain on the ballot in Assembly District 45, the California Secretary of State’s Office said. Jesse Gabriel, another candidate, also expressed skepticism.

By Kevin Modesti

A candidate seeking to replace a California assemblyman who quit after being accused of mistreating women has quit the race herself after the revelation that she faced a gender-discrimination lawsuit when she was a union executive.

The 2013 lawsuit included the salacious allegation that Stevens told an employee assigned to attend a meeting with thenLos Angeles Mayor Antonio Villaraigosa: “We both know that the only reason you’re getting this assignment is that you have bigger boobs.”

In a message emailed to supporters Friday that blamed “dirty politics,” Samantha Stevens said she is suspending her campaign for the April 3 special election for the west San Fernando Valley seat vacated by Assemblyman Matt Dababneh, who resigned amid a sexual-misconduct scandal.

Stevens, a political consultant who lives in Reseda, wrote that “two prominent Valley political players” tried to “bully” her into getting out of the race earlier this month when they confronted her with the lawsuit, which has embarrassing implications for a candidate who entered the race in December with a call to female empowerment.

Stevens later said in an interview that the two men are Los Angeles City Councilman Bob Blumenfield and his campaign consultant Larry Levine, who support candidate Tricia Robbins Kasson, a Blumenfield aide and Levine’s client.

Blumenfield and Levine said in interviews that they met with Stevens before Robbins Kasson entered the Assembly District 45 race, and after another potential candidate they favored, L.A. Community College District Trustee Andra Hoffman, opted not to run for the Assembly. They said they approached Stevens as friends and former employers offering helpful advice to leave the race before news of the lawsuit harmed her reputation.

“It’s sad,” said Blumenfield, who said he learned of the lawsuit when copies of court documents arrived at his office by mail from an unknown source. “I don’t know anything about what [in the lawsuit] is or isn’t true, but I know enough about politics to know this isn’t good if you’re running for office in 2018, because this is the year of sexual harassment issues.”

The suit, filed in L.A. County Superior Court by former Service Employees International Union Local 721 political coordinator Rudy Gonzalves against SEIU, Stevens and others, alleged that Gonzalves was harassed and fired after he complained about discrimination against other employees based on gender, age and family status.

The suit was settled in 2015, and terms were not disclosed. A confidentiality agreement prevented Gonzalves and his attorney from speaking about the case when the Daily News contacted them this week.

In court documents, Gonzalves alleged that Stevens, then the SEIU’s director of governmental relations, assigned employee Susan Naranjo to attend a a 2012 meeting with Villaraigosa even though the subject was outside Naranjo’s area of expertise.

Gonzalves alleged Stevens told him she had “pimped out” Naranjo at the demand of SEIU President Bob Schoonover, because Schoonover believed Villaraigosa liked “eye candy.”

The suit claimed Naranjo was “devastated at the degradation of being assigned due to her physical attractiveness as if she were chattel, and the subsequent degradation of being referred to as ‘the Villaraigosa girl.'”

Villaraigosa is running for California governor. His campaign did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit separately claimed Stevens judged candidates for jobs and promotions based on their marital and parental status, downgrading those who had families.

Gonzalves claimed he was fired in 2013 because he complained about these and other actions.

Stevens, one of 140 women in California government who signed an open letter in October decrying sexual harassment in the California capital, said in her message to “friends and supporters” Friday that the matter was “an old lawsuit filed against my former employer by a disgruntled employee and, as his supervisor, I had also been named.”

In a phone interview, Stevens said Gonzalves was fired for poor performance and that she wasn’t involved in his dismissal.

She said he put her name on the suit because he was angry about bad performance reviews she had given him.

“The accusations in the lawsuit are not true,” said Stevens, who resigned from SEIU in 2015 for reasons she said were unrelated to the lawsuit. She said the decision to settle the suit was made by SEIU and she went along because fighting would have been too expensive.

Saying she had considered herself the front-runner, Stevens said efforts to discredit her because of the lawsuit would make it harder for her to raise the campaign funds she would need to be competitive in April. Last week, the SEIU declined to endorse Stevens or any other candidate in Assembly District 45.

“For over 30 years in government and politics, I’ve been inspired by courageous women who have had the determination and foresight to run for office against the odds and make a difference. Valley’s Tricia Robbins Kasson, a Blumenfield aide, runs for Dababneh’s Assembly seat

By Kevin Modesti

Tricia Robbins Kasson thinks electing a woman to replace Matt Dababneh in the California Assembly would be a big step toward curtailing sexual harassment in the state capitol.

Even better, the Democrat says, would be electing a woman with the economic-development experience needed to address one of the west San Fernando Valley’s biggest challenges.

Robbins Kasson, 46, a Tarzana resident who touts her work on downtown and west Valley revitalization as a Los Angeles City Council staffer, has declared her candidacy for the Assembly District 45 seat left vacant when Dababneh resigned after being accused by multiple women of sexual misconduct.

Other candidates include Democrats Jesse Gabriel, Samantha Stevens and Ankur Patel, and Republican Justin Clark. A special election has been set for April 3, with a runoff June 5 if nobody gets an outright majority. It’s one of four special elections for state legislative seats on those dates.

“I think I’m qualified to bring jobs and economic opportunity to the Valley, and to change the culture in Sacramento,” Robbins Kasson said in an interview.

Referring to the resignations of Dababneh and Assemblyman Raul Bocanegra and the investigation of state Sen. Tony Mendoza, D-Artesia, over sexual harassment charges, Robbins Kasson said this a moment for overdue change. “It’s time to have more women in positions of authority,” Robbins Kasson said. “We’ve done our work. Women are graduating from college as never before. We’re qualified, we’re capable.

“I believe when you have more women who are part of the conversations, it shifts the conversations.” A 2017 graduate of Emerge California, a program that recruits and trains Democratic women to run for office, Robbins Kasson said she didn’t plan to run for the Dababneh seat and planned to support L.A. Community College Trustee Andra Hoffman. Then Hoffman opted not to run for the Assembly, so Robbins Kasson jumped in.

Now Hoffman has endorsed Robbins Kasson, as has Bob Blumenfield, the area’s L.A. city councilman and former assemblyman, and Howard Berman, the former congressman.

As Blumenfield’s economic development deputy the past two years, Robbins Kasson has worked on creating programs to bring economic development to Sherman Way in Reseda and Canoga Park, “main street” areas that have suffered from the shift to mall shopping. Earlier, on the staff of City Councilman Jose Huizar, she worked on the Bringing Back Broadway revitalization.

Working for a private-sector public-policy consultant, she dealt with the Warner Center 2035 Specific Plan. If she’s elected to the state Legislature, Robbins Kasson said, she’ll work to help west Valley residents get good jobs by promoting educational and apprentice programs and access to child care.

A Chicago native whose family moved to the Valley when she was 6, Robbins Kasson attended Kennedy High but did not graduate. She earned a GED in 2002 before going on to Pierce and Mission community colleges and Santa Monica College, then Cal State Northridge for a bachelor’s degree in business administration and USC for a master’s in urban planning. Attorney Jesse Gabriel running for Dababneh’s Assembly seat

By Kevin Modesti

Jesse Gabriel, a Democratic attorney who has been fighting the Trump administration on behalf of young immigrants, has entered the race for Matt Dababneh’s old California Assembly seat representing the west San Fernando Valley. Gabriel, 36, an Encino resident, made the announcement Wednesday and asserted his prominence in the District 45 race by saying he has raised more than $300,000 in two weeks and is endorsed by state Sen. Ben Allen, D-Santa Monica. Gabriel is the fourth candidate to file a statement of intention to run. Others are Democrats Samantha Stevens and Ankur Patel and Republican Justin Clark.

A date has yet to be set by Gov. Jerry Brown for a special election to replace Dababneh, who resigned effective Dec. 31 after being accused of sexual misconduct by multiple women. Earlier, Raul Bocanegra resigned his Assembly seat in the northeast Valley following accusations of sexual harassment.

“I think we need to resist the bad public policy coming out of Washington, D.C., that’s going to be bad for Californians and really goes against our values,” Gabriel said in a phone interview. “And we need to think about things that are important to our community,” including environment, education, infrastructure and quality-of-life issues.

“Sacramento has enormous power to help address some of these issues. If the Trump administration is going to pull out of the Paris climate accords, then we as Californians can sign our own accords,” Gabriel said.

Gabriel, who grew up in the Ventura County community of Oak Park, moved to Encino from Santa Monica in July with his wife, Rachel Rosner, also an attorney. They have 2-year-old and 3-month-old sons.

Gabriel, a constitutional-rights and general-litigation attorney with Gibson, Dunn & Crutcher, said he has spent most of the past 10 months working on lawsuits seeking to protect undocumented young people known as Dreamers from Trump administration efforts to roll back Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) protections.

A Harvard law graduate, he was counsel to Sen. Evan Bayh, D-Indiana. Gabriel serves on the the Los Angeles County Commission on Local Government Services, and on the boards of the L.A. League of Conservation Voters and the Jewish Federation of Greater L.A.

Democrats enjoy a more than 2-1 edge over Republicans in voter registration in District 45. Dababneh’s and Bocanegra’s resignations, along with Sebastian Ridley-Thomas’ resignation last week for health reasons, has at least temporarily dropped Democrats below a two-thirds supermajority in the Assembly.

CapitolBeat by Jason Fox Election Fallout Plus: More Tax on Services, Tax Credit Bills W With the June primary election completed, campaigns across California will heat up now that the field of candidates has been narrowed. While there were no big surprises, there were a number of key races at the state and federal level that will impact California’s political landscape—and possibly the balance of power in Washington, D.C. As expected, Gavin Newsom was the top candidate in the governor’s race. The major focus was who would take the second spot to move to the November general election. John Cox, the leading Republican candidate, was able to capitalize on an endorsement from President Trump and move ahead of Democrat contenders Antonio Villaragosa and John Chiang. CPA and CalCPA member Fiona Ma took first place in the treasurer’s race and will face Republican Greg Conlon, also a CPA. Betty Yee and Xavier Becerra both moved to the general election and will likely be re-elected controller and attorney general, respectively. Orange County voters recalled Sen. Newman over his vote in support of the gas tax increase. Republican, and former Assemblymember Ling Ling Chang, was elected to replace him. With the swap from a Democrat to a Republican, this likely blocks the Democrat’s two-thirds supermajority in the Senate. The Democrats had used that supermajority to pass legislation that would enact new taxes, pass the state budget and submit constitutional amendments to the ballot without input from Republicans. In the Assembly Luz Maria Rivas (D) Jesse Gabriel (D) won special elections to fill vacant seats. For the primary races, most elections went as expected, except for Assemble District 76 in San Diego County. Republican Rocky Chavez left that seat to run for Congress and two Democrats were able to lock out Republicans from retaining the seat in November. On the federal level, Sen. Diane Feinstein cruised to the top spot for the U.S. Senate. Former Senate President pro Tempore Kevin De Léon, who is positioning himself as the progressive challenger to the moderate Feinstein, came in a distant second place. National political pundits speculated that California’s “top two primary” could result in democratic candidates splitting the vote and being shut out of the targeted congressional seats to strip control of the U.S. House of Representatives from the Republicans. That didn’t happen and those seats will be the focus of heavy campaigning this fall by Democrats. Sales Tax on Services A scheduled discussion in June on Senate Bill 993 (Hertzberg), which would enact a new 3 percent sales tax on business services and reduce the sales tax on goods by 2 percent, was postponed until later this summer. Legislative leaders plan to bring stakeholders together to provide additional information about the impact of a broad professional services tax on business activity. CalCPA and other business groups have opposed this measure and past services tax efforts; however, the topic continues to simmer. While it is unlikely something will move forward in the Legislature this year, with a new governor who will likely be more progressive taking office next year, there is a threat of tax reform—including a services tax—being discussed. CalCPA will continue to ensure CPAs have a seat at the table and provide the profession’s input. ‘Charitable’ Work-arounds Following the new federal tax reform, many high tax states, like California, continue to explore options for managing the impact on their taxpayers. Specifically, the $10,000 cap on state and local tax (SALT) deductions has inspired the introduction of Senate Bill 227 (De Léon) and Assembly Bill 2217 (Burke), which aim to circumvent this limit. Both bills have received bipartisan support and propose state sponsored charities that will collect taxpayer dollars in the form of a charitable contribution, rather than a tax payment, in exchange for a state tax credit. The expectation is that the taxpayer could then deduct the contribution from their federal taxes, which is not limited by the new SALT cap. SB 227 creates the California Excellence Fund, a state established charity, in exchange for a tax credit equal to 85 percent of the contribution. AB 2217 similarly allows a taxpayer to donate to a school district, which in turn funnels a portion of the money to the Treasurer’s office, which will them send the money to the general fund. In exchange, the treasurer provides the school district with credits and the district provides those credits to the donating taxpayer. The taxpayer may then claim a tax credit worth 80 percent of the face value of their initial contribution. Proposals such as these, which have passed in New York, Connecticut and New Jersey, raise many questions that would need to be addressed before tax practitioners could consider this option for their clients. Most importantly, it is unclear whether the IRS will allow these types of deductions. The IRS said it will be issuing specific guidance on how these types of credits will be treated and said “taxpayers should be mindful that federal law controls the proper characterization of payments for federal income tax purposes.” Many anticipate the IRS would not be willing to simply allow these types of deductions wholesale. Still, California leaders continue to explore options to skirt perceived negative impacts of the federal tax laws. This will continue to be a topic of discussion in 2018 and something tax practitioners should be mindful of when working with their clients in 2019. Jason Fox is CalCPA’s director of legislation. You can reach him at jason.fox@calcpa.org. Election 2018: Jesse Gabriel holding onto seat in race for West San Fernando Valley’s 45th District Assembly seat

By Elizabeth Chou

A Democratic incumbent is outpacing a Republican college student in early election results released Tuesday for a western San Fernando Valley district that stretches from Chatsworth to Calabasas.

The 45th district Assembly race is between Cal State University of Northridge political science major Justin Clark, and constitutional rights attorney Jesse Gabriel, who was elected to represent the district in a June special election. Gabriel was comfortably ahead of Clark, and appeared headed to a regular two-year term beginning Dec. 3. The pair also faced off previously in the June special election. Gabriel won that election, while Clark, the sole Republican, in the race garnering a quarter of the votes in the district.

* See the latest election results Gabriel, 37, has sued the Trump administration in two cases aimed at continuing protections under President Barack Obama’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals policy for people who illegally immigrated to the United States at a young age. His priorities goals include increasing access to a good education and protecting the environment. Gabriel is completing the remainder of the 45th district term that was left unfinished when the area’s previous representative, Matt Dababneh, stepped down following allegations of sexual misconduct. Shortly after assuming office, he was assigned a leadership role as an assistant whip for the Democratic majority.

Clark, a 19-year-old Calabasas resident who works at a local ice cream shop, says his goals if elected include tackling waste and corruption in state government.

While he is likely to lose the race, Clark said Tuesday evening that he would be “very proud” if his campaign garners similar results as in the primary election, or better. In the last election, the percentage of votes he brought in “easily beat Republican voter registration,” he said.

This was due to “our message of bipartisanship and focusing on the issues that matter most to local residents,” he said. “We put people ahead of politics. My only regret is that we lacked the funding to spread our positive message further then we did.”

He said that while his opponent was able to send out several mailers to voters, he and his campaign relied on walking neighborhoods and knocking on doors.

He said the “traditional avenues” for soliciting donations are often available to Republican candidates in California, because some would-be donors may feel that such candidates are not likely to win or they feel the party’s leadership is not strong enough.

Clark networked and went to family members for donations, but he recently got a boost from the Los Angeles Police Protective League, a union that represents rank-and-file police officers. The organization gave his campaign $4,400, the maximum that such an organization is allowed to give, he said.

Clark said that while going door-to-door in a Democratic-leaning district, he found that there were those who did not identify with his party, but who nevertheless said they would vote for him.

“I find that interesting,” he said. “But you can’t knock on every door in the district.”

The district Gabriel and Clark are seeking to represent includes the city of Calabasas, and the Los Angeles city communities of Chatsworth, West Hills, Canoga Park, Winnetka, Reseda and Northridge.

Credit: By Elizabeth Chou | echou@scng.com | Daily News

GOP California Assembly candidate blasted for campaign flier criticized as anti-Semitic

Andrew Sheeler

Nine Jewish California lawmakers, all Democrats, signed a letter Friday condemning Republican Tyler Diep’s campaign for releasing campaign literature depicting his opponent in the race for the Orange County-based 72nd Assembly District, Democrat Josh Lowenthal, in a fashion often seen in anti-Semitic fliers.

They join a number of rabbis, including Peter Levi, regional director of the Orange County chapter of the Anti-Defamation League, in criticizing the campaign handout, which shows Lowenthal clutching money while writing that he is out to “make a quick buck.”

“The images undoubtedly link him to the age-old, false and dangerous stereotype about Jews and money and Jews and greed,” Levi said.

> Our statement on the offensive campaign mailer against Jewish CA Assembly candidate @JoshLowenthal pic.twitter.com/cetEeThPVe
>
> — Assemblymember Jesse Gabriel (@JesseForASM45) November 2, 2018

Diep’s mailer is similar to one sent by Republican Connecticut state representative candidate Ed Charamut’s campaign — which shows his Jewish Democratic opponent, Rep. Matthew Lesser, “with a wide-eyed grin, clutching a wad of $100 bills,” according to CNN.

“We know the impact (these ads) have, particularly in the Jewish community,” Levi said.

“In this week when decent people throughout our nation are mourning the murders of Jews in their synagogue, a piece of campaign literature that depicts a Jewish candidate as an individual with a long nose and implying he is a habitual liar is utilizing historically anti-Semitic tropes,” said Rabbi Stephen J. Einstein in a statement released by a consultant for the Lowenthal campaign.

That statement also noted that Huntington Beach, in Orange County, is home to both the anti-Semitic “Rise Above Movement,” described by the Southern Poverty Law Center as “a racist, violent right-wing fight club” and the Institute for Historical Review, a prominent Holocaust denying organization.

It also comes as police investigate recent anti-Semitic vandalism at an Orange County synagogue.

“This is not a neutral district. Diep’s coded language is carefully calibrated to appeal to anti-Semites and racists in a last-ditch effort to save his campaign,” the Lowenthal campaign statement read.

The Diep campaign, in a statement to the Los Angeles Times, denied that the mailer was an anti-Semitic attack.

“Allegations to the contrary are despicable and incorrect. Tyler is Vietnamese and fled Communist persecution — he is highly sensitive to attempts at exploiting stereotypes to score political points,” the Diep campaign said.

אל הטקס גם הגיעו מכובדים רבים, ביניהם נציגים מהקונסוליה הישראלית ומשטרת לוס אנג'לס. שני חברי קונגרס מקומי הגיעו מהבירה, סקרמנטו. גם נציגים רבים מהרשות המקומית בלוס אנג'לס הגיעו, ביניהן נציגת ראש העיר, אריק גרסטי, הגברת טנאז גולשן.

דקות אחדות לפני שהחל הטקס המכובד, שוחחתי עם שירי וסרמן, מנהלת "מרכז שפר" של ה-IAC, שהסבירה איך מרימים אירוע כה גדול ומכובד בתוך מספר ימים: "היה לנו חשוב מאוד כארגון הישראלי-יהודי הגדול בארה"ב להביע תמיכה בעקבות הפיגוע, להזדהות עם הקורבנות ולגנות את האנטישמיות. עובדים במרץ מאז שעות הבוקר של יום ראשון כדי להזמין את הקהילה, רבנים, כמרים, נציגי LAPD, משרד ראש העיר, ועוד", היא אמרה. כאשר היא נשאלה על סידורי האבטחה בעקבות הפיגוע הרצחני, השיבה וסרמן כי "תמיד יש לנו אבטחה במקום. עם זאת, כן הגדלנו את כמות המאבטחים וישנה גם נוכחות משטרתית שבעצם גורמת לנו להרגיש יותר בטוחים".

בסביבות השעה 7:00 נפתחו הדלתות ומאות באי המקום התיישבו במקומותיהם. שולי לבב, תושבת האזור, סיפרה כי "הרגשתי שאני רוצה להיות פה ולהזדהות עם הכאב. כאשר שמעתי על האירוע ביום שבת, הייתי מאוד עצובה. עצוב לי שאנחנו כבני אדם לא יכולים לקבל כל אחד כפי שהוא. אחרי 16 שנים שבהן אני חיה פה, לא דמיינתי שאראה מחזה כזה. אני הולכת לבתי כנסת בשבתות, והפיגוע בפיטסבורג יגרום לי ללכת אפילו יותר. חשוב לי להיות מסוגלת להציג את היהדות שלי ללא חשש".

כאמור, נוכחות משטרתית גדולה נרשמה בטקס, ולא רק בפן האבטחתי. כריס פיצ'ר, סגן מפקד משטרת לוס אנג'לס באזור עמק סן פרננדו, ביקש להעביר מסר חשוב: "אני כאן כדי להדגיש בפני הקהילה היהודית והישראלית שהם בטוחים בבתי הספר, בבתי הכנסת ובכל המקומות האחרים", הוא אמר. מעבר לכך, פיצ'ר הסכים לספר מעט על ההיערכות המיוחדת של המשטרה בעקבות הפיגוע: "החלטנו לנקוט במספר צעדים, רובם סמויים, כדי לתגבר את האבטחה סביב מוסדות ישראלים ויהודים. אנחנו עובדים בתיאום מלא עם סוכנויות פדרליות, לרבות ה-FBI וה-ATF", הוא אמר. בהמשך, כשפיצ'ר עלה על הבמה כדי לנאום, הוא חזר על הדברים והדגיש את המחויבות המשטרתית לקהילה היהודית.

מטעם ראש העיר, אריק גרסטי, נשלחה טנאז גולשן אשר אמרה: "כולנו חיבקנו את ילדנו טיפה יותר חזק מתוך ידיעה שמה שקרה ב"עץ החיים" יכול היה לקרות גם פה. זה היה יום טרגי וקשה, אך עלינו להתאחד יחד כדי לגרום לשינוי. עלינו לעמוד בקול אחיד ולומר, 'אנחנו לא מפחדים ואותנו לא ישתיקו'. משפחות רבות יהודיות בארה"ב ובאירופה נאלצות להתמודד עם הסכנה האמיתית ששמה האנטישמיות. חובתינו כאמריקאים, כיהודים וכבני אדם להגיב לשנאה העיוורת באהבה בלתי פוסקת", היא אמרה.

סגן הקונסול הכללי של ישראל בלוס אנג'לס, איתן וייס, עלה על הבמה וסיפר על תחושותיו: "בגלל הנסיבות, אני עצוב שאני עומד מולכם. אבל בו בזמן אני חש גאווה לייצג את מדינת ישראל", הוא אמר והמשיך, "ישראל מכירה היטב את הטרור מעשרות השנים האחרונות, ואנחנו לא שוכחים שארה"ב תמיד הייתה שם בשביל לתמוך בנו. סייעתם לנו להתאבל, וכעת אנו מוצאים את עצמנו במצב הפוך בו אנו, אזרחי מדינת ישראל, תומכים בכם. בעודי מדבר, צוות של מומחים ישראלים ל-PTSD הגיעו לפיטסבורג כדי לסייע לקהילה, לקורבנות, לאנשי אכיפת החוק ואנשי הרפואה אשר חוו טראומה גם כן".

ג'סי גבריאל, הנציג של מחוז ה-45 (מערב עמק סן פרננדו) של קליפורניה בבית הנבחרים המקומי בסקרמנטו אשר גר באנסינו, פתח את דבריו בעברית ואמר: "קודם כל אני רוצה להגיד תודה רבה ל-IAC, זה מאוד חשוב שאנחנו פה ביחד בזמן הזה ובמקום הזה". לאחר מכן הוא שב לדבר באנגלית ואמר, "בתור יהודי שגר במשך שלוש שנים בישראל, זה מאוד משמעותי עבורי להיות כאן הערב. סגן המפקד פיצ'ר, אני רוצה להביע בפניך את אסירות התודה שלנו, יהודים תושבי לוס אנג'לס, לשוטרי ה-LAPD על העבודה הקשה שלכם. חשוב לי לציין שני דברים הערב: ראשית, עלינו להכיר שישנה עלייה באנטישמיות. הדור שלנו אינו חסין בפניה. אני חושב שרבים מאיתנו מרגישים את זה כהורים. שנית, המסורת שלנו מלמדת אותנו כיצד להגיב לאירועים מסוג זה. התגובה הכי טובה שאפשר לתת לשנאת חינם היא אהבת חינם. עלינו ללמד את הילדים שלנו לאהוב את יהדותם ולאהוב את מדינת ישראל. עלינו ללמד אותם להיות אמריקאים גאים ועלינו ללמד אותם להיות גאים במשטרה. לגור בארה"ב כיהודי גאה זו התגובה הכי טובה לאירועים מתועבים כאלה", הוא אמר.

ניכר היה בפני באי הטקס כי האירוע היווה סוג של סגירת מעגל עבורם. רבים שוחחו איתי על כך שהם התמודדו עם הפיגוע באופן אישי, או לעיתים עם המשפחה. אך האירוע אמש נתן להם את הבמה לפגוש באנשים דומים להם שעוברים את אותן החוויות. הייתה שאלה אחת שבחרתי לשאול את כל מי ששוחחתי איתו, והיא "האם האירוע בפיטסבורג יגרום לך שלא להגיע לבתי כנסת או למוסדות יהודים?". שלא יהיה צל של ספק, לא היה ולו אדם אחד שהשיב בחיוב.

-- Garcetti’s national rainmaking continues Tuesday with an event that’s back on his home turf but focused elsewhere.

Harnessing his connections to the entertainment industry glitterati — as he has before — the mayor is hosting a fundraiser for other state Democratic parties that will feature Jimmy Kimmel and DJ Khaled, seeking to raise $100,000 apiece for party organizations in California, Iowa, Nevada, New Hampshire, Michigan, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Ohio, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Cool Kid Flannery Branham-Kamp volunteers helping refugees, homeless

Seventeen-year-old Flannery Branham-Kamp has spent countless hours volunteering.

Friday, September 21, 2018

LOS ANGELES (KABC) -- Seventeen-year-old Flannery Branham-Kamp has spent countless hours volunteering.

Last weekend, she joined dozens of others filling 600 outreach kits for the homeless full of food, blankets and toiletries. She's also traveled to New Jersey to help refugees and immigrants seeking aid at a church near her grandmother's home.

"A lot of it was like getting houses ready for immigrants, and then meeting the families, taking them out, and getting them assimilated with the language," said Branham-Kamp.

The senior at Sierra Canyon School in Chatsworth has also co-founded a campus feminism club called FEVER, which stands for: Feminism Empowering Voice for Equality and Rights.

"We're doing a women's shelter drive this year and we're looking forward to being able to help all the kids in our school and also raise awareness about gender equality," said Branham-Kamp.

Branham-Kamp has enjoyed getting a first-hand look at politics while interning for State Assemblyman Jesse Gabriel. She says watching his constituents voice their concerns and impact laws introduced in Sacramento has had a big impact on her. This ABC7 Cool Kid now wants to study theater and gender and sexuality studies in college, hoping to make films that spotlight her work with refugees.

"If kids are being brought up in a world where films are representing these people, and showing them that they're good people, I think the world is going to be a much better place," said Branham-Kamp.
